evangelize: To instruct in the gospel; to preach the gospel to; to convert to Christianity; as, to evangelize the world. His apostles whom he sends To evangelize the nations. Milton.
evaporometer: An instrument for ascertaining the quantity of a fluid evaporated in a given time; an atmometer.
evangely: Evangel. (old) The sacred pledge of Christ's evangely. Spenser.
evaluate: To fix the value of; to rate; to appraise.
evincible: Capable of being proved or clearly brought to light; demonstrable. Sir. M. Hale. --E*vin"ci*bly, adv.
eversive: Tending to evert or overthrow; subversive; with of. A maxim eversive . . . of all justice and morality. Geddes.
evocate: To call out or forth; to summon; to evoke. Stackhouse.
evulsion: The act of plucking out; a rooting out.
evection: 1. The act of carrying up or away; exaltation. (old) Bp. Pearson. 2. (Astron.) (a) An inequality of the moon's motion is its orbit to the attraction of the sun, by which the equation of the center is diminished at the syzygies, and increased at the quadratures by about 1º 20'. (b) The libration of the moon. Whewell.
evilminded: Having evil dispositions or intentions; disposed to mischief or sin; malicious; malignant; wicked. -- E"vil-mind`ed*ness, n.
evermore: During eternity; always; forever; for an indefinite period; at all times; -- often used substantively with for. Seek the Lord . . . Seek his face evermore. Ps. cv. 4. And, behold, I am alive for evermore. Rev. i. 18. Which flow from the presence of God for evermore. Tillotson. I evermore did love you, Hermia. Shak.
eviternal: Eternal; everlasting. (old) -- Ev`i*ter"nal*ly, adv. Bp. Hall.
eventual: 1. Coming or happening as a consequence or result; consequential. Burke. 2. Final; ultimate. "Eventual success." Cooper. 3. (Law) Dependent on events; contingent. Marshall.
evolation: A flying out or up. (old) Bp. Hall.
evergreenstate: Washington; -- a nickname alluding to the abundance of evergreen trees.
evolute: A curve from which another curve, called the involute or evolvent, is described by the end of a thread gradually wound upon the former, or unwound from it. See Involute. It is the locus of the centers of all the circles which are osculatory to the given curve or evolvent. Note: Any curve may be an evolute, the term being applied to it only in its relation to the involute.
evincement: The act of evincing or proving, or the state of being evinced.
evilly: In an evil manner; not well; ill. (old) "Good deeds evilly bestowed." Shak.
everlasting: 1. Lasting or enduring forever; exsisting or continuing without end; immoral; eternal. "The Everlasting God." Gen. xx1. 33. 2. Continuing indefinitely, or during a long period; perpetual; | 1. Eternal duration, past of future; eternity. From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God. Ps. xc. 2. 2. (With the definite article) The Eternal Being; God. 3.
evict: 1. (Law) To dispossess by a judicial process; to dispossess by paramount right or claim of such right; to eject; to oust. The law of England would speedily evict them out of their possession. Sir. J. Davies. 2. To evince; to prove. (old) Cheyne.
evilness: The condition or quality of being evil; badness; viciousness; malignity; vileness; as, evilness of heart; the evilness of sin.
eventuate: To come out finally or in conclusion; to result; to come to pass.
evocative: Calling forth; serving to evoke; developing. Evocative power over all that is eloquent and expressive in the better soul of man. W. Pater.
evangile: Good tidings; evangel. Above all, the Servians . . . read, with much avidity, the evangile of their freedom. Londor.
evangel: Good news; announcement of glad tidings; especially, the gospel, or a gospel. Milton. Her funeral anthem is a glad evangel. Whittier.
evenness: The state of being ven, level, or disturbed; smoothness; horizontal position; uniformity; impartiality; calmness; equanimity; appropriate place or level; as, evenness of surface, of a fluid at rest, of motion, of dealings, of temper, of condition. It had need be something extraordinary, that must warrant an ordinary person to rise higher than his own evenness. Jer. Taylor.
eventerate: To rip open; todisembowel. (old) Sir. T. Brown.
evolatical: Apt to fly away. [Obs. or R.] Blount.
evangelist: A bringer of the glad tidings of Church and his doctrines. Specially: (a) A missionary preacher sent forth to prepare the way for a resident pastor; an itinerant missionary preacher. (b) A writer of one of the four Gospels (With the definite article); as, the four evangelists, Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
eventration: (a) A tumor containing a large portion of the abdominal viscera, occasioned by relaxation of the walls of the abdomen. (b) A wound, of large extent, in the abdomen, through which the greater part of the intestines protrude. (c) The act af disemboweling.
evincive: Tending to prove; having the power to demonstrate; demonstrative; indicative.
evenhanded: Fair or impartial; unbiased. "Evenhanded justice." Shak. -- E"ven*hand`ed*ly, adv. -- E"ven*hand`ed*ness, n.
eventful: Full of, or rich in, events or incidents; as, an eventful journey; an eventful period of history; an eventful period of life.
evet: The common newt or eft. In America often applied to several species of aquatic salamanders. [Written also evat.]
evangelistary: A selection of passages from the Gospels, as a lesson in divine service. Porson.
evade: To get away from by artifice; to avoid by dexterity, subterfuge, address, or ingenuity; to elude; to escape from cleverly; as, to evade a blow, a pursuer, a punishment; | 1. To escape; to slip away; -- sometimes with from. "Evading from perils." Bacon. Unarmed they might Have easily, as spirits evaded swift By quick contraction or remove. Milton. 2.
evanescence: The act or state of vanishing away; disappearance; as, the evanescence of vapor, of a dream, of earthly plants or hopes. Rambler.
evacuant: Emptying; evacuative; purgative; cathartic. -- n. (Med.) A purgative or cathartic.
evanescent: 1. Liable to vanish or pass away like vapor; vanishing; fleeting; as, evanescent joys. So evanescent are the fashions of the world in these particulars. Hawthorne. 2. Vanishing from notice; imperceptible. The difference between right and wrong, is some petty cases, is almost evanescent. Wollaston.
eviction: 1. The act or process of evicting; or state of being evicted; the recovery of lands, tenements, etc., from another's possession by due course of law; dispossession by paramount title or claim of such title; ejectment; ouster. 2. Conclusive evidence; proof. (old) Full eviction of this fatal truth. South.
eventilate: 1. To winnow out; to fan. (old) Cockeram. 2. To discuss; to ventilate. (old) Johnson.
eviscerate: To take out the entrails of; to disembowel; to gut.
evolutionary: Relating to evolution; as, evolutionary discussions.
everywhen: At any or all times; every instant. "Eternal law is silently present everywhere and everywhen." Carlyle.
evanish: To vanish. Or like the rainbow's lovely form, Evanishing amid the storm. Burns.
everywhere: In every place; in all places; hence, in every part; throughly; altogether.
evolution: 1. The act of unfolding or unrolling; hence, in the process of growth; development; as, the evolution of a flower from a bud, or an animal from the egg. 2. A series of things unrolled or unfolded. "The whole evolution of ages." Dr. H. More. 3. (Geom.) The formation of an involute by unwrapping a thread from a curve as an evolute. Hutton. 4. (Arith.
evaporable: Capable of being converted into vapor, or dissipated by evaporation.
evileye: . See Evil eye under Evil, a.
evaporate: 1. To pass off in vapor, as a fluid; to escape and be dissipated, either in visible vapor, or in practice too minute to be visible. 2. To escape or pass off without effect; to be dissipated; | 1. To convert from a liquid or solid state into vapor (usually) by the agency of heat; to dissipate in vapor or fumes. 2. To expel moisture from (usually by means of artificial heat), leaving the…
everglade: A swamp or low tract of land inundated with water and interspersed with hummocks, or small islands, and patches of high grass; as, the everglades of Florida. [U. S.]
evaporator: An apparatus for condensing vegetable juices, or for drying fruit by heat.
evidence: 1. That which makes evident or manifest; that which furnishes, or tends to furnish, proof; any mode of proof; the ground of belief or judgement; as, the evidence of our senses; | To render evident or clear; to prove; to evince; as, to evidence a fact, or the guilt of an offender. Milton.
evidentiary: Furnishing evidence; asserting; proving; evidential. When a fact is supposed, although incorrectly, to be evidentiary of, a mark of, some other fact. J. S. Mill.
evidently: In an evident manner; clearly; plainly. Before whose eyes Jesus Christ hath been evidently set forth. Gal. iii. 1. He has evidently in the prime of youth. W. Irving.
evanid: Liable to vanish or disappear; faint; weak; evanescent; as, evanid color. (old) They are very transistory and evanid. Barrow.
evasive: Tending to evade, or marked by evasion; elusive; shuffling; avoiding by artifice. Thus he, though conscious of the ethereal guest, Answered evasive of the sly request. Pope. Stammered out a few evasive phrases. Macaulay. -- E*va"sive*ly , adv. -- E*va"sive*ness, n.
eventuation: The act of eventuating or happening as a result; the outcome. R. W. Hamilton.
evaginate: Protruded, or grown out, as an evagination; turned inside out; unsheathed; evaginated; as, an evaginate membrane. | To become evaginate; to cause to be evaginate.
evert: 1. To overthrow; to subvert. Ayliffe. 2. To turn outwards, or inside out, as an intestine.
evangelism: The preaching or promulgation of the gospel. Bacon.
eventuality: 1. The coming as a consequence; contingency; also, an event which comes as a consequence. 2. (Phren.) Disposition to take cognizance of events.
evolve: 1. To unfold or unroll; to open and expand; to disentangle and exhibit clearly and satisfactorily; to develop; to derive; to educe. The animal soul sooner evolves itself to its full orb and extent… | To become open, disclosed, or developed; to pass through a process of evolution. Prior.
evoke: 1. To call out; to summon forth. To evoke the queen of the fairies. T. Warton. A requlating discipline of exercise, that whilst evoking the human energies, will not suffer them to be wasted. De Quincey. 2. To call away; to remove from one tribunal to another. "The cause was evoked to Rome." Hume.
event: 1. That which comes, arrives, or happens; that which falls out; any incident, good or bad. "The events of his early years." Macaulay. To watch quietly the course of events. Jowett (Thucyd. | To break forth. (old) B. Jonson.
evirate: To emasculate; to dispossess of manhood. (old) Bp. Hall.
evolutionism: The theory of, or belief in, evolution. See Evolution, 6 and 7.
evacuator: One who evacuates; a nullifier. "Evacuators of the law." Hammond.
evolutility: The faculty possessed by all substances capable of self- nourishment of manifesting the nutritive acts by changes of form, of volume, or of structure. Syd. Soc. Lex.
evaporative: Pertaining to, or producing, evaporation; as, the evaporative process.
evening: 1. The latter part and close of the day, and the beginning of darkness or night; properly, the decline of the day, or of the sum. In the ascending scale Of heaven, the stars that usher evening rose. Milton. Note: Sometimes, especially in the Southern parts of the United States, the afternoon is called evening. Bartlett. 2. The latter portion, as of life;
every: 1. All the parts which compose a whole collection or aggregate number, considered in their individuality, all taken separately one by one, out of an indefinite bumber. Every man at his best state is altogether vanity. Ps. xxxix. 5. Every door and window was adorned with wreaths of flowers. Macaulay. 2. Every one. Cf. Each. (old) "Every of your wishes." Shak.
eve: 1. Evening. (poetic) Winter oft, at eve resumes the breeze. Thomson. 2. The evening before a holiday, -- from the Jewish mode of reckoning the day as beginning at sunset. not at midnight; as, Christians eve is the evening before Christmas; also, the period immediately preceding some important event. "On the eve of death." Keble.
evangelicalism: Adherence to evangelical doctrines; evangelism. G. Eliot.
evangelistic: Pertaining to the four evangelists; designed or fitted to evangelize; evangelical; as, evangelistic efforts.
evener: 1. One who, or that which makes even. 2. In vehicles, a swinging crossbar, to the ends of which other crossbars, or whiffletrees, are hung, to equalize the draught when two or three horses are used abreast.
even: Evening. See Eve, n. 1. [Poetic.] Shak. | 1. Level, smooth, or equal in surface; not rough; free from irregularities; hence uniform in rate of motion of action; as, even ground; an even speed; an even course of conduct. 2. Equable;
evileyed: Possessed of the supposed evil eye; also, looking with envy, jealousy, or bad design; malicious. Shak.
evacuation: 1. The act of emptying, clearing of the contents, or discharging. Specifically: (a) (Mil.) Withdrawal of troops from a town, fortress, etc. (b) (Med.) Voidance of any matter by the natural passages of the body or by an artificial opening; defecation; also, a diminution of the fluids of an animal body by cathartics, venesection, or other means. 2.
everich: each one; every one; each of two. See Every. (old) Chaucer.
evagation: A wandering about; excursion; a roving. Ray.
everyday: Used or fit for every day; common; usual; as, an everyday suit or clothes. The mechanical drudgery of his everyday employment. Sir. J. Herchel.
evocation: The act of calling out or forth. Sir. T. Browne. The evocation of that better spirit. M. Arnold.
eversion: 1. The act of eversing; destruction. Jer. Taylor. 2. The state of being turned back or outward; as, eversion of eyelids; ectropium.
eventilation: The act of eventilating; discussion. (old) Bp. Berkely.
eventide: The time of evening; evening. [Poetic.] Spenser.
evergreen: Remaining unwithered through the winter, or retaining unwithered leaves until the leaves of the next year are expanded, as pines cedars, hemlocks, and the like. | 1. (Bot.) An evergreen plant. 2. pl. Twigs and branches of evergreen plants used for decoration. "The funeral evengreens entwine." Keble.
eventognathi: An order of fishes including a vast number of freshwater species such as the carp, loach, chub, etc.
evident: Clear to the vision; especially, clear to the understanding, and satisfactory to the judgment; as, the figure or color of a body is evident to the senses; the guilt of an offender can not always be made evident. Your honor and your goodness is so evident. Shak. And in our faces evident the sings Of foul concupiscence. Milton. Syn. -- Manifest; plain; clear; obvious; visible;
evenfall: Beginning of evening. "At the quiet evenfall." Tennyson.
evangelic: Belonging to, or contained in, the gospel; evangelical. "Evangelic truth." J. Foster.
evensong: A song for the evening; the evening service or form of worship (in the Church of England including vespers and compline); also, the time of evensong. Wyclif. Milton.
evolutional: Relating to evolution. "Evolutional changes." H. Spenser.
evil: 1. Having qualities tending to injury and mischief; having a nature or properties which tend to badness; mischievous; not good; worthless or deleterious; poor; as, an evil beast; and evil plant; | 1. Anything which impairs the happiness of a being or deprives a being of any good; anything which causes suffering of any kind to sentient beings; injury; mischief; harm; -- opposed to Ant: good.
evolvent: The involute of a curve. See Involute, and Evolute.
evince: 1. To conquer; to subdue. (old) Error by his own arms is best evinced. Milton. 2. To show in a clear manner; to prove beyond any reasonable doubt; to manifest; to make evident; to bring to light; to evidence. Common sense and experience must and will evince the truth of this. South.
everything: Whatever pertains to the subject under consideration; all things. More wise, more learned, more just, more everything. Pope.
everych: each one; every one; each of two. See Every. (old) Chaucer.
eventless: Without events; tame; monotomous; marked by nothing unusual; uneventful.
everlastingness: The state of being everlasting; endless duration; indefinite duration.
evilfavored: Having a bad countenance or appearance; ill-favored; blemished; deformed. Bacon. -- E"vil-fa`vored*ness, n. Deut. xvi. 1.
evanesce: To vanish away; to because dissipated and disappear, like vapor. I believe him to have evanesced or evaporated. De Quincey.
eventually: In an eventual manner; finally; ultimately.
evolutionist: 1. One skilled in evolutions. 2. one who holds the doctrine of evolution, either in biology or in metaphysics. Darwin.
evangelization: The act of evangelizing; the state of being evangelized. The work of Christ's ministers is evangelization. Hobbes.
evaporation: 1. The process by which any substance is converted from a liquid state into, and carried off in, vapor; as, the evaporation of water, of ether, of camphor. 2. The transformation of a portion of a fluid into vapor, in order to obtain the fixed matter contained in it in a state of greater consistence. 3. That which is evaporated; vapor. 4. (Steam Engine) See Vaporization.
evectics: The branch of medical science which teaches the method of acquiring a good habit of body. (old)
evangelical: 1. Contained in, or relating to, the four Gospels; as, the evangelical history. 2. Belonging to, agreeable or consonant to, or contained in, the gospel, or the truth taught in the New Testament; | One of evangelical principles.
evasion: The act of eluding or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogation; artful means of eluding. Thou . . . by evasions thy crime uncoverest more. Milton. Syn. -- Shift; subterfuge; shuffling; prevarication; equivocation.
ever: 1. At any time; at any period or point of time. No man ever yet hated his own flesh. Eph. v. 29. 2. At all times; through all time; always; forever. He shall ever love, and always be The subject of by scorn and cruelty. Dryder. 3. Without cessation; continually. Note: Ever is sometimes used as an intensive or a word of enforcement. "His the old man e'er a son" Shak.
evolvement: The act of evolving, or the state of being evolved; evolution.
evernic: Pertaining to Evernia, a genus of lichens; as, evernic acid.
evenly: With an even, level, or smooth surface; without roughness, elevations, or depression; uniformly; equally; comfortably; impartially; serenely.
evolatic: Apt to fly away. [Obs. or R.] Blount.
evacuate: 1. To make empty; to empty out; to remove the contents of; as, to evacuate a vessel or dish. 2. Fig.: To make empty; to deprive. Evacuate the Scriptures of their most important meaning. Coleriage. 3. To remove; to eject; to void; o discharge, as the contents of a vessel, or of the bowels. 4. To withdraw from; to quit; to retire from;
everliving: 1. Living always; immoral; eternal; as, the everliving God. 2. Continual; incessant; unintermitted.
evidential: Relating to, or affording, evidence; indicative; especially, relating to the evidences of Christianity. Bp. Fleetwood. "Evidential tracks." Earle.. -- Ev`i*den"tial*ly, adv.
evacuative: Serving of tending to evacuate; cathartic; purgative.
